# zumime

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zumime/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zumime/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zumime/gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zumime/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

A file's name says what someone hopes it is; its bytes say what it is. An
upload named `invoice.pdf` can be a PNG, a `.docx` is a ZIP archive inside,
and a `.csv.gz` holds a CSV you cannot see until you open the gzip. Before
a parser starts, you want to know which of these you have, and whether the
file is encrypted or cut short.

zumime answers from both signals in one call and says whether they agree.
It needs no other package at run time and no system library, so it gives
the same answer on every machine.

* **The browser's algorithm.** The byte answer is the
  [WHATWG MIME Sniffing Standard](https://mimesniff.spec.whatwg.org/), with
  its supplied type, no-sniff flag and contexts, checked against Go's
  `net/http` sniff cases.
* **Containers and R's own files.** ZIP entry names tell a Word document
  from a JAR, and ISO base media brands tell an M4A from an MP4, checked
  against the fixtures of the JavaScript
  [file-type](https://github.com/sindresorhus/file-type) package. RDS,
  RData, Parquet, SQLite, Stata and SPSS files are known by their headers.
* **A hierarchy.** Every type has a parent, ending at
  `application/octet-stream`, so an unknown ZIP-based format is still a ZIP,
  and an allowlist of `"image"` accepts every image.
* **What to know before opening.** Encryption, completeness, line endings
  and a script's interpreter, read from the same bytes, and the type inside
  a compression wrapper, from the name or, with
  [zukomp](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zukomp), from the decompressed
  bytes.
* **The same answer everywhere.** No `mime.types`, no Windows registry, no
  libmagic: the extension table is generated from IANA's registry and
  Apache httpd's `mime.types`.

## Installation

Install zumime from CRAN:

``` r
install.packages("zumime")
```

Or install the development version from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zumime")
```

## Usage

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zumime)
```

Take a folder of uploads: a real PDF, a PNG that claims to be a PDF, a
compressed CSV and an R data file.

```{r}
uploads <- tempfile("uploads")
dir.create(uploads)
writeLines("%PDF-1.7", file.path(uploads, "report.pdf"))
writeBin(as.raw(c(0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a)),
  file.path(uploads, "invoice.pdf"))
con <- gzfile(file.path(uploads, "sales.csv.gz"), "w")
writeLines(c("region,total", "north,10"), con)
close(con)
saveRDS(mtcars, file.path(uploads, "cars.rds"))

paths <- list.files(uploads, full.names = TRUE)
```

`mime_type()` types each file from its bytes and from its name. `agree` is
`FALSE` for the PNG named `invoice.pdf`, and `inner` names what the gzip
holds, guessed from the `.csv` before the `.gz`:

```{r}
files <- mime_type(paths)
files$path <- basename(files$path)
files[c("path", "type", "by_name", "agree", "inner")]
```

`mime_check()` asks only the allowlist question, from the bytes alone,
since that is the question you ask because names lie. Of the two files
named `.pdf`, one is:

```{r}
setNames(mime_check(paths, "application/pdf"), basename(paths))
```

`mime_sniff()` runs the standard on bytes in hand, as a browser would on a
response. A `text/plain` label is one some servers send for anything, so
the standard checks it and finds binary bytes; under `nosniff` the label
stands:

```{r}
png <- readBin(file.path(uploads, "invoice.pdf"), "raw", 8)
mime_sniff(png, type = "text/plain")$type
mime_sniff(png, type = "text/plain", no_sniff = TRUE)$type
```

Types form a hierarchy, so a question about a family covers its members:

```{r}
docx <- "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document"
mime_parent(docx)
mime_is(docx, "application/zip")
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
unlink(uploads, recursive = TRUE)
```

Every function but `zumime_info()` starts with `mime_`, and every type it
returns is a canonical name from the registry that `mime_types()` lists.

## Learn more

* [Checking an upload before you open it](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zumime/articles/checking-an-upload.html)
  walks through an allowlist, the `agree`, `encrypted` and `complete`
  columns, and the incremental sniffer on a stream's first chunk.
* The [reference](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zumime/reference/) documents
  every function, grouped by task.

## Related work

The byte answer follows the WHATWG MIME Sniffing Standard and is tested
against Go's `net/http` sniff cases; `mime_parse()` is tested against the
web-platform-tests `mimesniff` fixtures. Container inspection follows
[file-type](https://github.com/sindresorhus/file-type),
[filetype](https://github.com/h2non/filetype) and
[mimetype](https://github.com/gabriel-vasile/mimetype); the extension table
is generated from the [IANA media types
registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/) and Apache httpd's
`mime.types`. zumime's code is written from these references, not copied
from them. The test suite uses Go's sniff cases and file-type's answers as
oracles, credited where they are used.
